newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour urges IRA truce now, then talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour urges IRA truce now, then talks.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party, which could assume responsibility for troubled Northern Ireland if it wins a general election on May 1, urged the IRA on Saturday to call a truce now to get its Sinn Fein spokesmen into peace talks.

Labour's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, Mo Mowlam, told the British Broadasting Corporation that, if the Irish Republican Army called an immediate truce, Sinn Fein, its political wing, could take part in Belfast peace talks which resume on June 3.

She said such a truce would have to be called "pretty speedily" to allow time for the British government to verify that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) had ended all activities related to its war against British rule.
"If they show by word and deed that they are committed to the democratic process then we think they ought to safely move into the talks process," she said.

Mowlam's statement was seen signifying that there would be little change to Britain's Northern Ireland policy if Labour beats Prime Minister John Major's Conservative party, which is faring badly in national public opinion polls, in May.

Major's government says Sinn Fein, which seeks to reunite Northern Ireland with the Irish republic, is welcome to the talks once a verifiable IRA ceasefire is in place. The IRA has rejected any preconditions.

Mowlam said a British government would be satisfied that the ceasefire was genuine if targeting, surveillance and training ended and if there was a halt to IRA vigilante-style "punishment beatings" of minority Roman Catholics in the British province.

She was speaking the day after the IRA claimed responsiblity for last Wednesday's twin bomb attacks on a railway network near Wilmslow in northwestern England which severely disrupted traffic but caused no casualties.
The attack, the first in mainland Britain since last year, was seen as an attempt by IRA to get Northern Ireland on the British election agenda, where it ranks scant attention.

The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year accusing the British government of placing impossible conditions on the entry of Sinn Fein into peace talks such as a commitment by the guerrillas to start disarming.
Pat Doherty, the Sinn Fein vice-president, told the BBC he welcomed Mowlam's remarks but he gave no hint of the likelihood of a new IRA truce.

Doherty said that he and party president Gerry Adams thought there could be a new IRA truce if the British government set a date for Sinn Fein's entry into peace talks with Protestant Unionists, who want the province to stay British.

He also repeated Sinn Fein's demands that a future British government set a time frame for the talks, drop all preconditions and authorise "confidence-building measures" thought to include the release of IRA prisoners.
Doherty called on the Labour party to meet Sinn Fein at official level, something the British and Irish governments refused to do until the IRA ends its war against British rule.
